articles.text: Editor: We’ve lived in town for over 20 years and like many of our neighbors, we chose Piedmont over other East Bay cities for its strong public schools. Resources no doubt account for a good part of PUSD’s success. Voter-backed local school taxes and a generously endowed foundation supplement state funding, helping maintain facilities, student-support services, and extracurricular activities. Without its dedicated and talented teachers, though, Piedmont – despite its wealth and widely shared commitment to education – might have attractive campuses, but it wouldn’t have the schools that drew folks to town in the first place. The Association of Piedmont Teachers has been working fairly and openly to secure a decent contract for its members, even as the district pleads poverty and pushes teachers toward direct action. Piedmonters eager to protect what truly makes the town rich, and who want security for all the major players in their kids’ everyday lives, would do well to support APT’s campaign. Piedmont teachers make PUSD a regional standout. Fair compensation, including wages and benefits commensurate with the tremendous value our teachers bring to town, is the least we owe them. –Matthew M. Goldstein, Ph.D. Laura E. articles.text: To be a Super Bowl quarterback is to be famous. The average American may not be able to name the United States Secretary of State, yet it is more than likely that they can tell you that Brock Purdy is the quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers and that Patrick Mahomes is the quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs, the two teams that played in tomorrow’s Super Bowl. An average citizen may also be able to tell you that both Purdy and Mahomes can be accurately described as young, poised and as having “good field vision.” These famous athletes see what their opponents are trying to do and, in the moment, respond accordingly. They make accurate, almost instantaneous, decisions based on the rapidly changing picture before them. This week’s gospel story, the Transfiguration of Jesus, gives three of his disciples, Peter, James and John, an opportunity, like Super Bowl quarterbacks, to develop and demonstrate good field vision; the occasion to see the big picture and to respond accordingly. On a mountain top away from the crowds, the three are given a vision of the eternal identity of their friend and teacher. Before their eyes his clothes become dazzling white, he engages in conversation with the quintessential law-giver Moses and the quintessential prophet Elijah. A cloud overshadows them and from the cloud a voice proclaims, “This is my Son, whom I dearly love. Listen to him.” Good field vision on their part was to recognize Jesus’ divine identity, and that he is the teacher of teachers, the prophet of prophets, that he is truly God in our midst. On that mountain top they are given the opportunity to see that Jesus does not stand apart from the tradition of the law and the prophets but is a living expression of that tradition. articles.text: The magical experience of talking with grown-ups No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling mind blown when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world - from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share in, but that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. We remember, often very clearly, how people made us feel when we were children. • An uncle who looked at your drawings and scribbles with an artist’s perspective, recognizing your use of shape, line and color • A neighbor who gave you the time to fully explain your thoughts and feelings, asking follow-up questions that showed you were really being heard • A teacher who pulled you aside to share that the assignment you turned in was more than good - it left them awed and they want to know how you felt while working on it These adults made us feel like we were more than ‘just a kid’. Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. So how do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising coming from a camp director, but I recommend sending them to camp. Photo by Sebastián León Prado The relationship between a grown-up and child is very important. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. Wonderful, magical, kind, kidsat-heart counselors and staff who we hired for their innate ability to see children for the wonders they are. Not perfect angels or naive brats, but smallish humans who have their own unique interests, attributes and lenses through which they see the world. keeping our ratios tight (camper to staff 1:2 overall and 1:5 in cabins), we create opportunities every day for a camper to experience the magic of being seen. I am proud to report that we see those special moments all the time: an adult turning on their listening ears, seeing not ‘just a kid’, but a person they are happy to give their full heartfelt attention to. Affirmed. Interesting. Valuable. Creative. Loved. Special. Whatever wonderful feeling was felt, it was felt because someone took the time to help them feel the goodness that was already in themself. At Camp Augusta, we believe there is something awesome in every child, we need only to take the time to notice. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. has been Camp Augusta’s director for more than 20 years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and program philosophies can be found at www. campaugusta.org. This article originally appeared in the Post on February. 1, 2023. pages.text: Wednesday, February 14, 2024 9 Piedmont Play Schoolers host Lunar New Year parade By Oriana Syed Piedmont Play School, a cooperative preschool located at Hampton Park, held its Annual Lunar New Year Parade on Friday, February 9. Dressed in red, the children walked hand in hand with their teachers and caregivers around the field. Leading the parade was teacher Raven Ritchie in a dragon costume that the kids Kids made their own cut-out dragon masks for the parade. Preschoolers made a dragon costume for teacher Raven Ritchie to wear. Preschool teacher Raven Ritchie leads the parade dressed as a dragon. made for her earlier in the week. The parade was the culmination of a week of exploring how Lunar New Year is celebrated around the world. “At Piedmont Play School we value teaching children about various cultures and traditions. It is important for us to recognize not only our classroom community but the greater community around us,” said Ritchie. While much of the focus this past week was on Chinese New Year, the preschoolers also learned about Lunar New Year celebrations in other countries. Ritchie talked about the differences in celebratory garments for the new year and noted how celebrations can be similar but unique. “We try our best to share about different cultures respectfully through the use of examples through books, videos and crafts,” she explained. The children decorated personal masks for the parade and collaborated on making the lead dragon head constructed from boxes, paper, and embellishments. One child, who herself celebrates Lunar New Year at home, shared with Ritchie how happy she was to be celebrating this most special day at school. “Making the dragon head together as a class was a fun and engaging way to show our appreciation for the beautiful holiday that is Lunar New Year,” said Ritchie. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team claimed both of its final games of the season to share the league championship with Bishop O’Dowd with a 7-1 league record. The Highlanders bowled over San Leandro 74-24 on Wednesday, February 7 at Binks Rawlings Gym for Senior Night, and dominated Castro Valley 62-34 two days later at the Trojans’ gym. As a result, Piedmont was moved up to the Open Division of the North Coast Section playoffs and given a No. 6 seed. PHS will host No. 3 Carondelet on Thursday, February 15 at Binks Rawlings Gym and gain an automatic bid to the CIF State Tournament. The Highlanders were awarded a home-bid by the draw from a hat by the league’s athletic directors. The Highlanders celebrated its six seniors at the start of Wednesday’s game: Natalia Martinez, Lindsey Wirgler, Sam Smith, Kat Melian, Erinn Gardere, and Arshiya Ranjitkar. Martinez put on a dazzling show with 40 points against San Leandro and Castro Valley, including a perfect 10 for 10 three-pointers against the Pirates, a Piedmont school record. “The rim was on fire. I knew I wasn’t going to miss and if I was going to miss, it’d be a contested shot. I just thought, ‘I’m gonna keep shooting.’ From the beginning of the game, I knew I was on fire. I thought, ‘Just keep shooting like Stephen Curry.’,” said Martinez. Martinez goes down as one of Piedmont’s leading scorers in the company of Courtney Paris, Ashley Paris, Casey Morris, and Trinity Zamora. “I remember my freshman year with Kai [Johnson] being the only senior. I remember beating O’Dowd. Having Kai step up as the only senior made me want to do that when it was my time as a senior. All the players who were here before me really paved the way,” said Martinez. Wirgler joined the team as a junior but had to sit out last season due to transfer rules. She entered the starting lineup this year to become the team’s second leading scorer. “It’s been an up-and-down journey, but I’m glad to be here with this crew. Most importantly, we just have to finish this year out, we’ve been working way too hard to celebrate now. For me, my journey here has been different and I’ve been able to grow throughout every year of high school. Being a senior, I’m grateful to just be at the point where I can reflect back on how I’ve gotten here,” said Wirgler. “It’s a culmination as a long but fast four years. It’s great to look back at all that’s happened and be able to celebrate. Joining last year with such a strong team, I didn’t get a lot of playing time, but I learned a lot from that experience and put in work over the summer. To be able to have a role with only five people, it’s an opportunity very few people have and to have the success we do,” said senior Sam Smith. 62-33 over Castro Valley Piedmont trailed 12-11 through the first quarter but dominated after that. PHS went up 31-19 and then scored 14 points and allowed 11 in the third, 45-30. The Highlanders allowed just three points in the fourth, scoring 17. articles.text: Highlanders in NCS playoffs on Friday Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s soccer team honored its nine seniors on Senior Night: (front) Charlotte Davies (left), Hailey Marshburn, Lily Caldwell, Malea Hartford, Elle Ruegg; (back) Sara Broach, Amy Derr, Lola Biehn, and Clio Salzer. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team capped its highly successful season with an exciting 2-1 win over rival Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 6 at the recently reopened Witter Field. They held Berkeley to a scoreless draw on Friday, February 9, bringing their record to 11-2-3 (W-T-L) overall and 5-2-3 in league, second place behind Castro Valley. Entering the post-season North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 7 seed, Piedmont walloped No. 10 Albany 5-0 last night, February 13, in the first round. The Highlanders celebrated their nine seniors on the roster before the O’Dowd game: Charlotte Davies, Amy Derr, Hailey Marshburn, Lily Caldwell, Sara Broach, Lola Biehn, Malea Hartford, Elle Ruegg, and Clio Salzer. 1-0 draw with Berkeley In a back-and-forth match, Berkeley kept a defensive look causing Piedmont to have trouble finding rhythm on the attack. The Yellowjackets assigned its top defender, Camila Vasquez, on Piedmont’s Elsa Wallway, resulting in limited looks at goal from the aggressive freshman forward. The result meant Castro Valley captured the WACC’s Foothill Division title and Piedmont tied with Berkeley for second place in the league. 2-1 over Bishop O’Dowd Coach Dan Chubbock started the game with all of the seniors, subbing in lead attackers Miranda Liu and Wallway after 10 minutes. Quickly after Liu and Wallway entered the pitch, Piedmont drew its first chance when Juliana Thornborrow weaved through the defense to send a pass out wide to Elle Ruegg. The right back sent in a low cross to Liu charging toward net, but the Dragons’ defender got a foot on the ball before colliding with Liu. Liu had another look later in the first half on some great interplay. Louisa Symokowick sent a laser pass to Thornborrow, who flicked a pass on a first touch to Liu running in behind. Liu’s shot was stopped on a foot save by BOD’s keeper, and the score remained 0-0 at halftime. At the 50th minute, Piedmont broke the deadlock after Wallway drew a penalty kick. It come moments after she beat multiple defenders to draw a free kick on the left side of the penalty area. Wallway took the initial free kick, sending a cross that was returned to her via a defensive header. Retrieving the ball, Wallway patiently waited for two defenders to come her way, darting to the right, before intricately moving into the box and drawing contact on her back by the over pursuing defender. Wallway calmly buried the PK at the right post. With 10 minutes left in the game, Bishop O’Dowd tied the game. Players celebrate on the field in the final moments of their 2-1 win over Bishop O’Dowd. It was their first game at Witter Field this season.

We fought until the end and it was unfortunate to concede with less than 10 minutes to go,” said coach Todd Sullivan following the loss to Berkeley. Thursday’s game was a milestone for Sullivan, who has coached the Highlanders in 150 games since being named head coach. Based on the success of the team, they were promoted from the Shoreline Division to the more competitive Foothill Division during his time at the school. “Even Berkeley’s coach at the end praised us for coming back from 2-nil down to O’Dowd. articles.text: Seeing my brother at the starting line shaking, I wonder what it’s like. The shot goes off. He’s gone. The speed he pedals at is something foreign to me; the fighting spirit that he possesses is unknown to me. After tens of minutes he comes around the final stretch. I see him finish – dead last. The months of training all for nothing. Day after day, week after week, he didn’t seem himself. “Is this normal?” I asked myself. “Is he ok?” This concept of mental pain felt very distant to me. I had never gone through it. Once I joined crew, I learned that competing in sports isn’t just a physical battle, it’s a mental one, too. Mental struggles of professional athletes In 1989, Clint Malarchuk, an NHL goalie had his jugular vein cut by a skate during a game. He survived this injury and was somehow able to come back a few weeks later. While this side of the story has a happy ending, Malarchuk was mentally destroyed. It was a trauma undiagnosed. In the years to come, he started drinking and taking painkillers regularly. Back then, mental health struggles were often viewed as a sign of weakness than an illness and where seeking help wasn’t an option. You fight through the pain silently. In 2008 when Malarchuk attempted suicide, it wasn’t taken lightly. That was the turning point where coaches and fans realized the pain athletes were going through. Acknowledgement of this topic began to reduce the number of struggling athletes, but a significant percent of them still suffer from burnout, depression, or anxiety. One of the big reasons is the competitive environment and social stigmas. The feeling of having to do the same thing day after day or even loss after loss takes so much mental fortitude. Having to adjust your lifestyle to be aligned with your team can be a daunting task. While professionals are on a completely different spectrum of athletic ability, there are obvious connections regarding mental health when compared to an everyday athlete. As a high school rower, I’ve seen how these struggles relate to my experiences. I often find myself thinking about not doing as much as I should have. However, to counteract this, Luca Vieira, now a college athlete, advised me: “Convince yourself you’re the best.” An athlete’s take on the topic Luca is a rowing coxswain at UC Berkeley. He and his team have secured multiple titles including at Henley Royal Regatta, one of the largest and most popular races in the world. Regattas are the pinnacle in rowing, as each crew prepares tirelessly for months on end to compete for a mere six minutes. The best way to keep going in races is in his words, “Convince yourself that you’re the best”. Having self confidence is the mindset that is key to winning. Luca’s ‘open book’ relationship with his coach has been one of the most valuable to him, and the key to that is to not be afraid of asking questions. His most important priority is keeping focused on his boat and not the other boats. When you are not ‘In the zone’ the boat feels much more out of sync and affects your overall speed. Emotional maturity is extremely important because the inability to hold back whatever comes to mind can create rifts in the team, leading to a loss of focus. Making a Difference As a young athlete, I’m passionate about spreading awareness about mental health challenges. I want to use my voice to help people care about this issue. We each have the power to make a real impact and it starts with us, the young athletes. Evrim Duransoy is a Sophomore at PHS and is a rower on the Oakland Strokes varsity team.

Parking at East Bay MUD’s Valle Vista Staging Area, the Kings Canyon Loop is a moderately challenging trail that walks alongside the Upper San Leandro Reservoir. Hiking the loop requires 6.4 miles of walking and around 950 feet in elevation gain. The reservoir is the highest it’s been in years, providing fantastic views for the majority of your hike. Walking along the northern portion of the reservoir, there’s a continuous great view of the rolling East Bay hills as you walk along the winding trail. It’s a great location for birding A close view of the San Leandro Reservoir from the Kings Canyon Loop Trail Staff Photos The San Leandro Reservoir is the highest it’s been in years thanks to recent rains. The final portion of the Kings Canyon Loop Trail with the San Leandro reservoir to the left California newts can be spotted walking along the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Electricity towers are overhead on the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Watch out for several muddy and slick areas on the trail. The Kings Canyon Loop trail brings hikers underneath groves of Oak trees. or catching sight of little critters. On multiple occasions, California newts were spotted passing by on the trail. As for the difficulty of the trail, about 75 percent of the trail was manageably flat, but once you hit the 4.5 mile mark, the trail noticeably ramps up in elevation gain—providing 460 feet in ascent in just half a mile – so roughly half of the day’s elevation gain is in one portion of the trail. It’s worth mentioning that about 10 sections of the trail were oversaturated and muddy, making it difficult to walk through without slipping. Be advised to use caution and patience when passing over slippery surfaces. After walking alongside the reservoir for those 4.5 miles, the trail takes into the hills and narrows down from over 10 feet wide to just a few feet in some sections. It traverses underneath groves of Oak trees and eventually provides an overhead view of the reservoir. At the 6-mile mark, you come to an intersection to continue on the Kings County Loop Trail to your left or to an added trail, Rimer Creek Trail to the right. The Posts’ suggestion is to take the trail on the left which leads back to the reservoir. The trail on the right adds a mile to your afternoon of hiking, but featured some of the most saturated portions of mud throughout the day. Despite being a magnificent trail, it is severely underrated. In 7.5 miles of hiking around noon on a Saturday, The Post passed just 21 other hikers.

articles.text: On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. United States, 1984) — a contemporary envisioning of a Chinese mother goddess, rendered in a dangling complex of ceramic forms — mingle interrogations of utopian ideals, the experience of migration, and what it means to be a woman protagonist. Fresh approaches to well-established genres also boldly defy expectations. What appears to be a traditional Chinese landscape painting by Wu Chi-Tsung (b. Taiwan, 1981) is in fact formed from sculptural layers of crumpled photosensitive paper, while an experimental film by TT Takemoto (b. United States, 1967) peers beneath the surface of documentary footage of Japanese American women factory workers to reveal an intimate social atmosphere. “At a moment of heightened turmoil domestically and around the globe, Into View feels so needed right now, entwining concepts like mythology, cosmology, political uprisings, social intimacy and ecology as viable alternatives to our current systems and empowering audiences to rethink possibilities in their own lives,” said Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art & Programs Naz Cuguoglu. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org. articles.text: A new exhibition at the Legion of Honor showcases the history of San Francisco through fashion. Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style features iconic collections of 20th and 21st-century women’s fashion in the United States and the Bay Area. The exhibition includes over 100 pieces, some loaned by local collectors of haute couture. It is the first major presentation of the museum’s own costume collection. A wide range of fashion is represented, from French dressmakers to Japanese avant-garde designers. Designs by Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, Christopher John Rogers, Comme des Garçons, Rei Kawakubo, Kei Ninomiya, Junya Watanabe, Yohji Yamamoto and Rodarte are on display. “These garments echo the evolving urban landscape of San Francisco, a city populated by structures that push the confines of modern architecture, likewise made by advanced engineering and with state-of-the-art industrial materials,” said Laura Camerlengo, curator of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Fashioning San Francisco is on display through August. Visit https://www.famsf.org/exhibitions/fashioning-san-francisco to learn more. Fashioning San Francisco features over 100 clothing items from famous designers.

Into View at Asian Art Museum By Selen Ozturk On view through October 17, Into View: New Voices, New Stories is an exhibition of recent acquisitions by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco that disrupts the dominant narratives of contemporary art by bringing the fantasies, joys, sorrows and yearnings of Asian American and Asian diaspora artists into vibrant dialogue with one another to challenge common conceptions of Asian art history. Through paintings, sculptures, ceramics, prints, video, and mixed-media works, this unique presentation places different time periods, genres, and political and social concerns into one exhibit, reimagining art world conventions to reflect this group of primarily women and LGBTQ Asian artists. Many of the included works are from artists from the Bay Area or with ties to the region. Throughout the exhibition, works from prominent local voices join past and present via a reclamation of traditional imagery. For instance, Heroine by Rupy C. Tut (b. India, 1985) — a painted reimagining of a scene from Punjabi folklore — and Nuwa’s Hands by Cathy Lu (b. United States, 1984) — a contemporary envisioning of a Chinese mother goddess, rendered in a dangling complex of ceramic forms — mingle interrogations of utopian ideals, the experience of migration, and what it means to be a woman protagonist. Fresh approaches to well-established genres also boldly defy expectations. What appears to be a traditional Chinese landscape painting by Wu Chi-Tsung (b. Taiwan, 1981) is in fact formed from sculptural layers of crumpled photosensitive paper, while an experimental film by TT Takemoto (b. United States, 1967) peers beneath the surface of documentary footage of Japanese American women factory workers to reveal an intimate social atmosphere. “At a moment of heightened turmoil domestically and around the globe, Into View feels so needed right now, entwining concepts like mythology, cosmology, political uprisings, social intimacy and ecology as viable alternatives to our current systems and empowering audiences to rethink possibilities in their own lives,” said Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art & Programs Naz Cuguoglu. The Asian Art Museum (200 Larkin St.) is open Thursdays from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m., and Fridays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 ages 65 and up, $13 ages 13 to 17 and college students) are available at asianart.org. articles.text: American Conservatory Theater premieres Big Data onstage at the Toni Rembe Theater tomorrow, February 15. Written by Kate Attwell and directed by ACT’s Artistic Director and Tony Award winner Pam Mackinnon, Big Data is a modern-day love story awash in technology and the dizzying possibilities of artificial intelligence. The play follows four young people. Sam loves Timmy, and Lucy loves Max, but they all succumb to the addiction of technology and smart devices. When Sam and Lucy’s parents make Michael Phillis stars in Big Data. a shocking announcement, the family is forced to confront the technology that has distracted them from each other and the legacy they’ll leave behind. MacKinnon and Attwell reunite to bring this revolutionary piece to audiences, inspired by Attwell’s experience touring search engine platform Mozilla’s “Glass Room” pop-up interactive exhibit in San Francisco. The cast includes Gabriel Brown, Rosie Hallett, Julia McNeal, Michael Phillis, Harold Surratt, Jomar Tagatac and BD Wong. The play will be performed through March 10. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/2023-24-season/big-data/. Kronos Quartet will perform at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on March 2.
articles.title: Big Data premieres on stage at ACT tomorrow

articles.text: Jazz vocalist Dianne Reeves will perform four concerts at SF Jazz Thursday through Sunday, February 22 - 25. A Grammy Award winner, Reeves is noted for her scores of R&B, gospel, Pop, Latin and Blues tracks and is considered one of the most proficient jazz vocalists today. She draws inspiration from Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday. Reeves has released numerous albums since 1987. Her most recent recorded album was Beautiful Life in 2014. Two years later she was recognized by the National Endowment for the Arts as the 2018 Jazz Master, the nation’s highest honor in the genre. Reeves continues to tour, most recently with the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra and Samara Joy, performing American jazz standard and holiday classics. All performances begin at 7 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/23-24/dianne-reeves/. Jazz vocalist Dianne Reeves to perform at SF Jazz for four evenings February 22-25.

articles.text: Renown quartet celebrating 50th year on March 2 The internationally acclaimed Kronos Quartet celebrates its 50th anniversary with a performance on Sunday, March 2, at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley. Entitled Five Decades, the program features the world premiere of Segara Gunung (Ocean-Mountain), a Cal Performances co-commissioned work by composer Peni Candra Rini, as well as excerpts from Michael Gordon’s gfedcba, a new work written for the group. Other music includes Severiano Briseño’s El Sinaloense (The Man from Sinaloa) arranged by Osvaldo Golijov, Sofia Gubaidulina’s Quartet No. 4, Steve Reich’s Triple Quartet, and Nicole Lizée’s ZonelyHearts, a multimedia work. An introductory eight-minute film by Sam Green, titled Kronos at Fifty will be shown. Founded in Seattle in 1973, Kronos Quartet has received more than 40 awards, including three Grammy Awards and the Polar Music, Avery Fisher, and Edison Klassiek Oeuvre Prizes. More than 1000 works have been written for the group, which has been praised for the inclusiveness of its repertoire. Kronos Quartet is the most well-known and nationally recognized string quartet that hails from San Francisco. Quartet members are David Harrington and John Sherba (violin), Hank Dutt (viola), and Paul Wiancko (cello). To purchase tickets, visit https://calperformances.org.
articles.title: Kronos Quartet returns to Zellerbach Hall

articles.text: Oakland Ballet will present its third annual Dancing Moons Festival March 14 through April 6 at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland and ODC Theater in San Francisco. The program is choreographed by all-Asian American Pacific Islander talent and will include a preview of the dance company’s Angel Island Project with choreography by Natasha Adorlee and Feng Ye. The project took inspiration from poetry carved by detainees held at the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station held thousands of immigrants through 1910 and 1940, mainly from China, Japan, India and the Philippines. “With captured imaginations, we take on a flight of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved in the walls by detainees,” Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig said. “The Angel Island Project helps us to trace who we are today by remembering from where we came.” Several selections will also be presented at the festival as works in progress, including Layer Upon Layer by Caili Quan (2022), Ballet des Porcelaines or The Teapot Prince by Phil Chan (original 1739; reimagined 2021), and highlights of Exquisite Corpse by Elaine Kudo, Seyong Kim, and Phil Chan (2023). For the first time since the festival’s inception, an exhibition of visual artists will be displayed at the cultural center. Artists include Asian Americans Sanjay Vora, Mark Shigenga and JaYing Wang. Performances on March 14-16 will take place at the Asian Cultural Center in Oakland. The performances on April 5-6 will take place at the ODC Theatre in San Francisco. To purchase tickets, https://oaklandballet.org/dancing-moons-festival/. Oakland Ballet’s Dancing Moons Festival takes place in Oakland and San Francisco this Spring.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet Dancing Moons Festival begins March 14

articles.text: This column usually sings the praises of musicians and concerts. Not this time. Seiji Ozawa died the other day. He was a flamboyant conductor, to be sure. In fact, he was one of the most prominent conductors in the world of music. I, however, was not a fan of his. This is a column that could have been written in 1970. I attended one of Seiji Ozawa’s concerts with the San Francisco symphony in the Opera House. The Orchestra was on stage, ready to begin the concert. Ozawa ran onto stage as if he had been poked in the backside. He leapt to the podium and without acknowledging the applause or his musicians, he began to conduct. He gesticulated like a man insane. I thought he was imitating a rabbit suffering convulsions. The musicians of his orchestra looked bewildered. Perhaps he impressed some of the unsophisticated in the audience. Ozawa’s career continued to the stratosphere. His salient features as a conductor were precision of attack. He was concerned entirely with attack and little else, it seemed. articles.text: Frank Langella as David Frost and Michael Sheen as Richard Nixon in Frost/Nixon Richard M. Nixon, the only U.S. president ever to resign from office, sat down with David Frost for a series of interviews several years after Nixon had resigned from office. Frost, whose career had taken a downward turn, needed a sensational moment that would bring him back into the spotlight. Nixon, living in exile in San Clemente, California, was eager to have the opportunity to find himself once again stage center in hopes of having the opportunity of if not at redemption, then certainly at putting his own spin on what had come to be known as Watergate – a harrowing and breathtaking scandal which had eventually brought down his administration. Who would have thought that this protracted interrogation would make not only good theater (the Broadway play was written by Peter Morgan), but also good filmmaking. In essence, Frost/Nixon is a prolonged conversation in which the two men face off in the living room of a suburban Los Angeles home. Where’s the drama in that? And yet, there is a palatable tension as the Nixon-Frost camps negotiate first the payment ($600,000) for the interviews with Nixon’s agent, Swifty Lazar (Toby Jones), and then the interviews themselves. Nixon, like a veteran prizefighter, bobs and weaves, selling his legacy like a hustler on a used car lot, while Frost tries to lay a glove on him without much luck. At least not initially. What makes the film remarkable is Frank Langella’s performance as Nixon. It’s a stunning piece of acting. Langella does not so much impersonate Nixon, he interprets the man’s mannerisms: his hunched, forward leaning walk; his deep, resonant voice; the jowly, perspiring visage, eyes shifting, assessing. Langella completely inhabits the character and creates a Nixonesque persona that is both powerful, believable and tragic. From almost the first frame, it is Nixon on the screen and Langella has vanished completely. Michael Sheen accomplishes the same thing, though his interpretation of Frost is less a physical presence and more the personification of Frost: carefully coiffed television personality, toothy smile, affable, made famous by his compelling interviews with famous people. Does Frost ultimately get the “get” he so desperately needed, one that would in effect be the trial that Nixon escaped due to Gerald Ford’s blanket pardon? Or does Nixon manage to turn the interviews into his bid for national absolution while making his case that he was a statesman of considerable accomplishments both domestically and internationally (Nixon did open the door to China). Therein is the tension in the film, two men using the reductive power of television as they joust, mano a mano. No matter the outcome, it is evident that Nixon was a brilliant politician who was fatally flawed. His life is reminiscent of a Greek tragedy, the pain of the years etched in his face, and that of his wife, Pat Nixon, who appears in one strained scene. Though he reached the pinnacle of power, Nixon was never able to free himself from the pathologies that framed his entire life, from those tenacious feelings of inferiority that loomed whenever he encountered the Brahmins of politics, perhaps best represented by John Kennedy. As Henry Kissinger was reported to have said of Nixon, “Imagine what he might have become had someone loved him.” Frost/Nixon. Directed by Ron Howard. Starring Frank Langella, Michael Sheen, Toby Jones and Rebecca Hall. Docudrama. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated R. Released in 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/ prime/apple tv.

articles.text: Perhaps it’s time to banish that all too familiar line, “This is a chick flick;” no matter that the genre is still alive and well in Hollywood. Yet there are also films about women who live very different lives and have very different definitions of what completes them. Case in point would be It’s Complicated. This is a woman’s movie to be sure; however, the target demographic is women 40 and older. Nancy Meyer (Baby Boom, Something’s Gotta Give, The Holiday) has been writing and directing romantic comedies about mature women for the better part of two decades. Her protagonists have had enough life experience to make insightful comparisons (that was then, this is now), bridling when things begin to feel hauntingly familiar. It’s Complicated has at its center the incomparable Meryl Streep, portraying Jane Adler, divorced for over a decade from Jake, played by Alec Baldwin. As a middle-aged woman, Jane has it all – a gorgeous, semi-rural home in Santa Barbara; a prosperous, up-scale bakery and café; three grown children; and is an accomplished chef. But still no man in her life. And therein is the rub. At her son’s NYU graduation (the whole family gathers in Manhattan), she unexpectedly has drinks and dinner with Jake with much dancing before and after. Jake is attending the ceremony without his younger wife, Agness (Lake Bell) – buff and demanding and the mother of 5-year-old Pedro. Drunk, swept away by familiar emotions and alcohol, they fall into bed and into an affair resurrecting all kinds of issues that long ago had resolved, or at least buried. Jane is suddenly the other woman and completely unhinged by events. Jake is energized, captivated and even jealous of Jane’s casual flirtations with her architect, Adam (Steve Martin). The situation makes for engaging comedy. What Meyers does, and does well, is focus on a certain type of woman – mature, professional, once wounded, affluent and feeling she has been sleeping alone for far too long. Jane’s circle of friends, all contemporaries, equally attractive, are at first shocked when told about Jake; yet they remain supportive. Meyer is adept at creating a world that is more fantasy than reality, possessing a bright patina, a bit Disneyesque, lacking any semblance of grit and inspired, it seems, by Crate and Barrel, Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin in It’s Complicated

articles.text: What can be enriching, even surprising, is to watch a foreign film and be immediately struck by the profound differences that exist between cultures – some deeply subtle, others far more blatant, evident in interactions, mannerisms, the scaffolding of life itself, all so unique and so compelling. Departures offers the audience such an opportunity for it constructs a tender and at times unsettling bridge between the living and the dead. Briefly, the film tells the story of Daigo (Mashiro Motoki), a young cellist and member of the Tokyo Symphony Orchestra. He is married to Mika (Ryoko Hirosue). Unexpectedly, the orchestra is disbanded and Daigo and Mika return to the prefecture of Yamagata and to his old family home, which he inherited when his mother passed away. He must find work and opportunities for cellists are rare. He answers an ad in a newspaper for a “departures” assistant. Thinking it’s a travel agency, Daigo goes to the office to apply. What he discovers is that the job is for a “departed” assistant, and the position entails “encoffination” of the deceased, an elaborate ritual of washing and dressing a loved one and then slowly placing the body into a coffin as the grieving family and friends look on. Daigo is at first repelled by the work, so much so that he Mashiro Motoki in a scene from Departures can’t share with Mika what the job involves. But he is also touched by the profound tenderness that his mentor, Mr. Sasaki (Tsutomu Yamazaki), exhibits as each step is slowly carried out. He is also struck by the impact this ceremony has on the family – the ritual is a gift, a farewell, a closure. American critics have faulted Japanese films for being overly sentimental, and Departures has its moments. But it is also beautifully acted and courageous in its intent. When it won an Oscar for Best Foreign Film, there was an audible gasp from those who believed it was not the best of a strong field; the voting Academy, however, disagreed. If a film has the power to touch the audience, to elicit an emotive response, then it has achieved far more than most films. And the willingness of director Yojiro Takita to explore this subject intimately, while telling the story of how two young people come to terms with Daigo’s work is compelling from the first frame. Departures explores a facet of the human condition from which we almost reflexively turn, away and it does so with insight and subtlety. Departures. Directed by Yojiro Takita. Starring Masahiro Motoki, Tsutomu Yamazaki, Ryoko Hirosue, Kazako Yoshiyuki. In Japanese with English subtitles. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on VUDU. In this wildly colorful mix is embedded a nice message that stresses that not everyone has to like the same thing or do the same stuff. It offers a deep, saturated ruby/purple color as well as a big, sweet bouquet of blackberries, cherry liqueur, licorice, wood and dried herbs. articles.text: Ken Li & Valerie Ng will celebrate 40 years of marriage on February 29. Piedmonters Ken Li and Valerie Ng have been married for nearly 40 years but will only be celebrating their 10th anniversary at the end of this month. They were married on Leap Year’s Day in Texas in 1984. Li, a prominent figure in town with decades of experience piloting the Piedmont Scouting Venture Scout program and Ng, a medical doctor, don’t usually make a fuss of celebrations or Valentine’s Day. However, with their once-in-every-four-year anniversary on the rise, they decided to reminisce their tale of courtship to the Post. They met in Dallas in the spring of 1982 after being set up for a blind date by a friend on Ken’s soccer team, and a classmate of Valerie. Their first date was anything but common. Valerie was in the middle of finals week for medical school and was letting off some steam with a pack of 10 classmates. Ken was invited to join, to see a matinee of Conan the Barbarian. “My group is pretty rowdy. It’s a Rocky Horror Picture Show with every movie. So we went to see Conan, and we were yelling and screaming,” recalled Valerie. “She shows up and I’m expecting to just meet her, but she shows up with like nine guys and her,” said Ken. “Then we go up to the theater to the front row and they have to sit all in a row in the front row. They start heckling at the movie while we’re watching.” Valerie remembered the day well, laughing about mocking Arnold Schwarzenegger’s deaf display of acting. “My thought was, if he could tolerate me and my friends, he had potential,” Valerie said with a smile. Ken survived the trial. They had a real date after that. A year and a half later, they were living together and an idea came to Ken. “It was February 28th and it was a leap year. And so I said, ‘Hey, wouldn’t it be cool to get married on a Leap Day?’” Ken recalled. T hey b ot h l i ke d t he impromptu idea. “So I go to work and I tell the secretary, ‘I’m taking the afternoon off to get married,’” said Ken. Ken, who grew up outside of Boston, and Valerie, who grew up in Oakland, were married in Texas on the spur of the moment. The couple relocated back from Texas to the West Coast for Valerie’s medical residency. They found a place in Piedmont, and started a family, and the rest is history. Ever since, Valerie has tirelessly worked, building an impressive medical career as a pathologist. Ken, similarly, shows high devotion to the Piedmont Scouting program and Piedmont Community Service Crew. For their 40th anniversary the couple will celebrate by Valerie taking a one-week vacation. Whether they refer to it as their 40th or 10th anniversary, their longevity is admirable. What is their secret? “I would just say we are not demanding of each other,” said Valerie. “I think that’s right, we do things together, but we can entertain ourselves so, there’s not a lot of pressure,” said Ken with a smile.
articles.title: Ken Li & Valerie Ng – a Leap Year’s Day marriage

articles.text: Neil and Beverly Rothenberg have been married for nearly 48 years. Beverly Rothenberg will never forget the time her husband, Neil, took off running down the street in Berkeley on one of their first dates. “We were out one night and there was this woman who was walking nearby who had her bag stolen,” she said. “Neil goes tearing after the guy without even batting an eyelash.” The thief eventually ducked out of sight, but the memory stayed with Beverly. “His quick action, I thought, was something really admirable.” Neil and Beverly met at UC Berkeley in 1972. The two had seen each other around the tennis courts before. “I was on the team at Cal and Beverly played recreationally,” said Neil. “I think the first time, it was Beverly who asked me out.” “He said no,” laughed Beverly, so I invited him over for dessert.” “It was the second time,” he jumped in. “She invited me over for dessert when I accepted. I remember exactly what it was— apple strudel.” And so began Neil’s love of Beverly’s cooking. One of the first things he would come to love about her. The couple dated for three years before they were engaged. “And this time, it was definitely me asking her,” Neil confirmed. He proposed to Beverly in the kitchen of their Berkeley apartment while she was cooking dinner. Beverly agreed enthusiastically. “There was a lot of jumping up and down.” They were married in Southern California, at Neil’s parents’ house in Tarzana. A second reception was held in Oakland, so they could include as many of their friends and family members as possible. “We didn’t have very much money, so we did everything on the inexpensive side,” said Neil. “In fact, we had a judge come to the house to marry us. I remember my dad slipping him 50 bucks afterwards for performing the ceremony!” After 48 years of marriage, Neil and Beverly still admire much about each other. “I think my favorite thing is that she has always looked out for me. That no matter what, she’s always loved me,” said Neil. “And it’s good to have Beverly to talk to before I do anything rash,” admitted a man sometimes known for quick thinking and quick action. “Neil is really good with our kids,” said Beverly. “He was the dad who did all of the coaching and the dad everybody knew at school. I admire that it was always important to him.” When asked if they had any Valentine’s Day plans, Neil and Beverly said they didn’t give the holiday too much thought these days. “There are so many more important things than just showing up one day a year,” said Beverly. “It’s the everyday things that you have to do. That’s way more important to me than flowers on a day.” Neil agreed wholeheartedly.

The two had seen each other around the tennis courts before. “I was on the team at Cal and Beverly played recreationally,” said Neil. “I think the first time, it was Beverly who asked me out.” “He said no,” laughed Beverly, so I invited him over for dessert.” “It was the second time,” he jumped in. “She invited me over for dessert when I accepted. articles.text: When Chad Olcott started dating Laura Pochop, the first thing he noticed was her mind. “If anyone knows my wife, she is the smartest person in the room wherever she goes,” he said. At the same time, Laura was falling in love with Chad’s voice. “The first things I realized I liked were his funny little accents and impressions,” she said. They had laughter, chemistry, and attraction. The stage was set for romance, with only one problem. They couldn’t tell anyone that they were dating. “It was a secret office romance,” laughed Olcott. “So, we had to be discreet.” Chad and Laura met at the non-profit organization City Year in 1993. He was Executive Director and she was Development Director. “It was this place that takes young people and puts them into full-time community service, kind of like an urban Peace Corps,” he explained. It was “a young, upstart company and a young office, filled with bad copiers and broken coffee machines,” he recalled, but also an office with the woman of his dreams in it. Together, they were asked to set up a branch of the company in Providence, RI, where they worked. Although they were in very different parts of the company – Laura’s work was administrative and Chad did mostly field work – the two eventually started spending time together after hours. As time went on, they developed a mutual respect and admiration for one another that blossomed into a relationship. On their first Valentine’s Day, the couple didn’t want to run into any trouble with their HR department, but Chad wanted Laura to know he was thinking of her. “So, I brought her favorite Dunkin’ Donuts iced coffee to her desk with three scoops of sugar,” he recalled. The only person who knew they were dating was their coworker and friend Lauren Dutton, now a Piedmont resident herself. After celebrating a milestone at work, Dutton pulled the two aside and asked them pointblank: “Is there something going on between you two?” The couple admitted gleefully. “And that’s how Lauren Dutton was there the first night we actually kissed,” recalls Chad. Chad and Laura moved into a small home in Providence in 1994. The stars aligned in 1995, and when Laura was accepted into the Stanford Graduate School of Business, a position opened up for Chad at City Year’s headquarters in San Jose. The two were West Coast-bound. In 1996, Chad and Laura were married at Hammersmith Farm in Newport, RI, a venue famous for being the location where John F. Kennedy and Jackie held their wedding reception. But Hurricane Fran made an appearance, and the event became windy and wet, but memorable. “It was the summer of Alanis Morrisette’s song “Ironic,” so everyone there was singing: ‘It’s like rain on your wedding day!’” These days, Chad and Laura usually opt for a more low-key Valentine’s Day celebration with a few friends over for a Valentine’s Day potluck this year. But that doesn’t mean the two are any less smitten with one another. “I love her smile and her dance moves,” said Chad. “And she’s an amazing cook.” “Nobody makes me laugh the way he does,” said Laura. “And he is a phenomenal father.” Photo by Chad Olcott Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop have been together for over thirty years. ®

articles.text: If you’re a business owner, you always have a lot to do and a lot to think about. But have you put much thought into how you’ll eventually leave it all behind? Even if you’re a few years away from that day, it’s a good idea to create an exit strategy. If you’re like most other owners, most of your net worth may well be tied up in your business – so how you exit that business can have a big impact on your finances and your retirement. As you begin the exit strategy process, you’ll need to examine some basic questions, such as how much you want for your business and how much it’s worth. But you’ll especially need to plan for the mechanics of your exit — that is, just how you’re going to sell or transfer ownership of it. Essentially, you have three main options: • Internal sale or transfer – You could sell or transfer your business to someone affiliated with the company, such as a family member, business partner or even a group of employees. The advantages of this method are that you’ll have greater control over the timing of your exit, and you’ll be able to provide greater continuity for your employees, clients and suppliers. One potential disadvantage is that your net sales proceeds may be less than what you’d get from selling the business to an unrelated third party. • External sale or transfer – The biggest benefit of selling or transferring your business to an unrelated third party is that you can potentially maximize your net sales proceeds. But you’ll need to consider some tradeoffs, too. For one thing, a sale to an outside person or business usually requires a long and possibly expensive due diligence process. Also, you’ll have less control over the timing of your exit than you would if you sold the business to an internal source. • Liquidation – If you liquidated your business by selling all your assets and shutting down operations, you could end up with far fewer net proceeds than if you sold the business to an internal or external source. However, you could raise cash pretty quickly. But if you chose to liquidate or dissolve your business, it could potentially be disruptive for your employees, clients and suppliers. Because everyone’s situation is different, there’s no clearcut formula for deciding which of these exit options is right for you. And it isn’t simply a matter of numbers, either, because you’ll need to consider some intangible factors, too. How will your family be affected by your choice? How would you feel if your business was in someone else’s hands, or no longer existed? You’ll need to work out these issues, along with the financial ones, before you decide on your business exit strategy. Fortunately, you don’t have to go it alone. You may want to consult your financial, legal and tax advisors, and possibly work with a commercial banker and a business evaluation expert. If you’re a business owner, you always have a lot to do and a lot to think about. But have you put much thought into how you’ll eventually leave it all behind? Even if you’re a few years away from that day, it’s a good idea to create an exit strategy. If you’re like most other owners, most of your net worth may well be tied up in your business – so how you exit that business can have a big impact on your finances and your retirement. As you begin the exit strategy process, you’ll need to examine some basic questions, such as how much you want for your business and how much it’s worth. But you’ll especially need to plan for the mechanics of your exit — that is, just how you’re going to sell or transfer ownership of it. Essentially, you have three main options: • Internal sale or transfer – You could sell or transfer your business to someone affiliated with the company, such as a family member, business partner or even a group of employees. The advantages of this method are that you’ll have greater control over the timing of your exit, and you’ll be able to provide greater continuity for your employees, clients and suppliers. One potential disadvantage is that your net sales proceeds may be less than what you’d get from selling the business to an unrelated third party. • External sale or transfer – The biggest benefit of selling or transferring your business to an unrelated third party is that you can potentially maximize your net sales proceeds. But you’ll need to consider some tradeoffs, too. For one thing, a sale to an outside person or business usually requires a long and possibly expensive due diligence process. Also, you’ll have less control over the timing of your exit than you would if you sold the business to an internal source. • Liquidation – If you liquidated your business by selling all your assets and shutting down operations, you could end up with far fewer net proceeds than if you sold the business to an internal or external source. However, you could raise cash pretty quickly. But if you chose to liquidate or dissolve your business, it could potentially be disruptive for your employees, clients and suppliers. Because everyone’s situation is different, there’s no clearcut formula for deciding which of these exit options is right for you. And it isn’t simply a matter of numbers, either, because you’ll need to consider some intangible factors, too. How will your family be affected by your choice? How would you feel if your business was in someone else’s hands, or no longer existed? You’ll need to work out these issues, along with the financial ones, before you decide on your business exit strategy. Fortunately, you don’t have to go it alone. You may want to consult your financial, legal and tax advisors, and possibly work with a commercial banker and a business evaluation expert. By drawing on several sources of expertise, you can feel more confident that you’ll make a decision that’s appropriate for your needs. One final suggestion: Don’t wait too long before you begin putting together your exit strategy. Time goes fast, and when the time comes for you to say goodbye to your business, you’ll want to be prepared. The group was pleased Karen Sullivan brought her husband, Tom Sullivan, to walk with them. Last week 16 hardy members of the Walking on Wednesdays group (and one K-9 best friend) showed up with raincoats and umbrellas. The group decided on a walk closer to the Exedra in case the rain got worse. They headed to the Hazel Lane loop and surrounding streets. The walkers went down Highland Avenue to its corner with Requa Road where they stopped for some history of the area. At the start of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have good educations, so she got Isaac Requa to build a one-room schoolhouse on his property at what is now the end of the Requa Place cul-de-sac. She hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children. This was the very first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Long leased the house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane. She also hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and California families, and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913. Soon after more classrooms and a gymnasium were added. The school had dormitory rooms for up to 70 students from first grade through high school. In 1924 there were 186 students, and in 1928 there were 21 teachers and 42 graduating seniors. However, the Stock Market crashed in 1929 and the following Depression created financial difficulties for many of the school’s parents. Piedmont High was less expensive and Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and the school closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The walkers passed the tall redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane, site of the entrance to the original Ransom Bridges School, The school itself was at what is now 141 Hazel Lane. They admired the Albert Farr craftsman design of the home and took a group photo in front of it. The walkers also noted the neighborhood’s first house at 152 Hazel Lane, and completed the rest of loop, which took them back to Requa Road. The group retraced their steps and decided that despite the rain they weren’t finished for the morning. They crossed Highland and went on Caperton Avenue to Mountain Avenue. The walkers sloshed down to Craig Avenue where they noted a beautiful Italian Victorian, built in 1883 and originally owned by Hugh Craig, Piedmont’s first mayor. Originally on Highland Avenue (then Vernal), the house was put on log rollers and pulled by horses to its current location, 55 Craig Avenue. The walkers went up Craig and found the somewhat secret back driveway to the Community Church. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge.
